usage: The new vehicle takes 로/으로, never 에서
to transfer at the transfer station
환승역 hwanseung-yeok is the official sign word at stations
Place of the action takes 에서, the destination vehicle takes 로
examples: 버스로 갈아타요.
I transfer to the bus.
Simplest frame: just the target vehicle + 로 + the verb
시청역에서 2호선으로 갈아타세요.
Please transfer to line 2 at City Hall station.
Everyday directions: 에서 marks where, 으로 marks which line
환승하려면 다음 역에서 내려서 갈아타야 해요.
To transfer you have to get off at the next station and change.
Real situation: pairs 내리다 then 갈아타다, the natural commuting sequence
nuance: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin (換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride') printed on every subway sign and announcement: 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트'). The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서 — English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에. Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.

usage: 안전하게 is the default adverb in road-safety phrases
잘하다 attaches to the noun 운전, splitting off the 하다
음주 운전 eumju unjeon is the fixed legal term for DUI
주다 adds the 'do me the favor' nuance
examples: 저는 운전해요.
I drive.
Bare statement; 운전 + 해요, the 하다 verb contracting to 해요
밤에는 천천히 운전하세요.
Please drive slowly at night.
Everyday advice: adverb 천천히 sits right before the verb
면허는 있는데 무서워서 아직 운전 못 해요.
I have a license but I'm scared so I still can't drive.
Real situation: shows the split negative 운전 + 못 + 해요
nuance: 운전하다 is Sino-Korean 운전 (運轉, 'move-turn', i.e. to keep a machine running) plus the light verb 하다, and it specifically means to operate a vehicle — primarily a car. Contrast it with 타다 'to ride/board', which is what a passenger does: the driver 운전해요 while everyone else just 타요. It is neutral in register and used by everyone, but the fixed compound 음주 운전 ('drinking driving') is the serious legal phrase you'll hear in warnings and news. Natural collocations include 안전 운전 (safe driving), 운전이 서툴다 (to be a clumsy driver), and 운전대를 잡다 (lit. 'grab the steering wheel' = to drive). Because it is a 하다 verb, the polite form is the irregular-looking but standard 운전해요 (하 + 여요 → 해요), and the negative and potential SPLIT the noun from 하다: 운전 안 해요, 운전 못 해요, never 안 운전해요. The English-speaker trap is exactly that splitting — and forgetting that the destination/route takes 까지 (집까지 운전해요) or 에서 for where the driving happens, since 운전하다 itself takes no direct object.

usage: to park in the parking lot
주차장 juchajang is the place; the spot itself takes 에
불법 주차 bulbeop juchain is the fixed term on tow-away signs
to look for a parking space
주차 + 공간 = parking space, a very common pairing
이중 ijung 'double-layer' describes the blocked-in row
examples: 여기에 주차해요.
I park here.
Simplest: location 여기 + 에 marks where the car ends up
지하 주차장에 주차했어요.
I parked in the underground parking lot.
Everyday: 지하 'underground' + 주차장, with past 했어요
자리가 없어서 길에 잠깐 주차해도 돼요?
There's no space so may I park on the street for a moment?
Real situation: asks permission with 해도 돼요 and the spot-marker 에
nuance: 주차하다 comes from Sino-Korean 주차 (駐車, 'halt-vehicle', i.e. to bring a car to a stop and leave it) plus 하다, so it means parking a vehicle, not stopping briefly to let someone out — that quick stop is 정차 (停車). Keep 주차하다 distinct from 세우다 ('to stand/stop something'): you can 차를 세우다 anywhere for a second, but 주차하다 implies leaving the car in a designated spot. Register is neutral and practical. The crucial particle point is that the resting place takes 에 (locative of where something settles), NOT 에서 (which marks where an action happens) — 주차장에 주차해요, never 주차장에서. Common collocations: 주차 금지 (no parking), 주차 요금 (parking fee), 주차 자리/공간 (a spot), 발레파킹 (valet). As a 하다 verb the negative and potential split the noun off: 주차 안 해요, 주차 못 해요. The English-speaker pitfall is the 에 vs 에서 choice and over-using a direct object — Koreans simply say 주차해요 and let context name the car.

usage: for the road to be congested
길 + 이 막히다 is THE everyday way to say 'traffic is bad'
차 here means 'traffic/cars' collectively, not one car
Same verb for blocked nose — a nostril is 'blocked' too
for the drain to be clogged
Pipes, sinks and drains all 막히다 when blocked
examples: 길이 막혀요.
The road is congested.
Core frame: 길 takes subject 이, the verb is intransitive
퇴근 시간이라 길이 많이 막혔어요.
The road was very jammed because it was rush hour.
Everyday: 퇴근 시간이라 'because it's leaving-work time' gives the cause
지금 출발하면 차가 막혀서 두 시간 걸릴 거예요.
If you leave now traffic will be bad and it'll take two hours.
Real situation: 막혀서 chains cause to the 걸리다 'take time' result
nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').

usage: to fall down on the street
Place of falling takes 에서, the action location
넘어져서 + 다치다 is the natural fall-then-injury chain
뒤로/앞으로 + 넘어지다 gives the direction of the fall
examples: 아이가 넘어졌어요.
The child fell down.
Simplest: subject 이, past tense, no place needed
빙판길에서 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요.
I slipped on the icy road and fell down.
Everyday: 미끄러지다 (cause) then 넘어지다 (result), the classic pair
할머니가 계단에서 넘어지셔서 병원에 가셨어요.
Grandmother fell on the stairs and went to the hospital.
Real situation: honorific -시- on 넘어지셔서 and 가셨어요 for an elder
nuance: 넘어지다 means a standing person (or upright thing) loses balance and topples to the ground, built on 넘다 'to go over' + -어지다 'to come to be', literally 'to come to fall over'. The line to draw is against 떨어지다 ('to fall FROM a height / to drop'): a person on their feet 넘어지다, but a cup off a table or a leaf from a tree 떨어지다 — and against 쓰러지다, which is to collapse from illness/exhaustion (fainting) rather than from tripping. Register is plain and used for everyone. The place where you fall takes 에서 (action location), and the cause is usually chained with -어서: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. Natural collocations: 넘어져서 무릎이 까지다 (scrape a knee falling), 넘어질 뻔하다 (almost fall), 넘어지지 않게 조심하다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 떨어지다 because English uses 'fall' for both — but 'I fell (down)' on flat ground is always 넘어지다; save 떨어지다 for dropping or falling off something.

usage: A fixed object you hit takes 에
A moving counterpart takes 과/와 (mutual collision)
The body part you knock takes 을/를
examples: 벽에 부딪쳤어요.
I bumped into the wall.
Simplest: stationary 벽 takes 에, past tense
급하게 가다가 어깨를 부딪쳤어요.
I bumped my shoulder while rushing.
Everyday: -다가 'while doing then', body part 어깨 takes 를
지하철에서 모르는 사람과 부딪쳐서 죄송하다고 했어요.
I bumped into a stranger on the subway and said sorry.
Real situation: 사람과 (mutual) + the social repair 죄송하다고 했어요
nuance: 부딪치다 means to strike or collide against something — a wall, a door, another person, or vehicle to vehicle. The particle does real work here: a stationary thing you hit takes 에 (문에 부딪치다), a body part you bang takes 을/를 (머리를 부딪치다), and a mutual collision with a moving party takes 과/와 (사람과 부딪치다). Beware the near-identical 부딪히다, which is the passive ('to be struck/run into by'): 차에 부딪히다 = 'to get hit by a car', so 부딪치다 vs 부딪히다 is the active-vs-passive divide, and learners constantly swap them. Do not confuse either with 만지다 ('to touch deliberately') — 부딪치다 is sudden and unintended impact. Register is plain. Collocations: 정면으로 부딪치다 (collide head-on), 세게 부딪치다 (hit hard), and figuratively 의견이 부딪치다 (opinions clash). The English-speaker pitfall is that 'bump into a friend' in English can simply mean 'run into = meet by chance' — that social sense is 우연히 만나다, NOT 부딪치다, which keeps its literal 'physical collision' meaning.

usage: Slippery surface takes 에서, where the slide happens
The textbook cause→result pair: slip then topple
to be careful not to slip
-지 않게 'so as not to' + 조심하다, a fixed safety frame
examples: 바닥에서 미끄러졌어요.
I slipped on the floor.
Simplest: surface 바닥 + 에서, past tense
비가 와서 길이 미끄러워요.
It rained so the road is slippery.
Everyday contrast: here the ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 'be slippery' describes the road
계단에서 미끄러질 뻔했는데 난간을 잡았어요.
I almost slipped on the stairs but grabbed the railing.
Real situation: -ㄹ 뻔하다 'almost' + the rescue 난간을 잡다
nuance: 미끄러지다 is the VERB 'to slip / slide / lose footing', describing the motion of your foot or body sliding on a slick surface. Mixing the two is the number-one English-speaker error here. Keep it apart from 넘어지다 too: 미끄러지다 is the slide itself, 넘어지다 is hitting the ground, and they chain naturally — 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. The slippery place takes 에서. Register is plain. Useful collocations: 발이 미끄러지다 (foot slips), 차가 미끄러지다 (a car skids), 미끄럼 주의 (the 'caution: slippery' floor sign, using the noun 미끄럼). The verb itself is regular (미끄러지다 → 미끄러져요), but its adjective cousin 미끄럽다 is ㅂ-irregular (미끄러워요), so don't carry the irregularity over.

Keep it apart from 넘어지다: 미끄러지다 is the slide itself, 넘어지다 is hitting the ground, and they chain naturally — 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요.
The verb itself is regular (미끄러지다 → 미끄러져요), but its adjective cousin 미끄럽다 is ㅂ-irregular (미끄러워요), so don't carry the irregularity over.

Its single most important confusion is with the look-alike ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 ('to be slippery'): the surface IS 미끄럽다 (길이 미끄러워요 — a state, ㅂ-irregular), but a person DOES 미끄러지다 (제가 미끄러졌어요 — an event). Mixing the two is the number-one error here.

Conjugating the verb like the ㅂ-irregular adjective: 미끄러워요 for 'I slip'. The verb 미끄러지다 is regular: 미끄러져요. Save 미끄러워요 for the adjective 미끄럽다.
Using 미끄러지다 alone when you actually fell down. Slipping is the slide; if you ended up on the ground, add 넘어지다: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요.

usage: 빨리 reinforces the urgency, a natural pairing
서둘러 acts adverbially before another verb
-ㄹ 필요 없다 'no need to', a calming fixed phrase
to make a mistake from rushing
-다가 chains rushing into the mishap it causes
examples: 빨리 서둘러요.
Let's hurry up.
Simplest: 빨리 + the 르-irregular polite form 서둘러요
늦어서 아침에 많이 서둘렀어요.
I was late so I hurried a lot in the morning.
Everyday: past 서둘렀어요 shows the doubled ㄹ of the 르 irregular
천천히 해도 되니까 서두르지 마세요.
You can take your time, so please don't rush.
Real situation: contrast 천천히 vs 서두르다, with the soft command 서두르지 마세요
nuance: 서두르다 means to hurry / rush / get a move on, acting on yourself to do things fast because time is short. Distinguish it from 급하다, the ADJECTIVE 'to be urgent / be in a rush' (마음이 급해요 = 'I feel rushed'): 급하다 describes the pressured state, while 서두르다 is the action you take in response — you 서두르다 because something is 급하다. It is plainly conjugated speech, fine in any everyday register, and softens to a gentle 서두르지 마세요 ('don't rush') when reassuring someone. The grammar heart of this word is that it is a 르 irregular: before a vowel ending the 르 sheds its ㅡ and an extra ㄹ appears, so 서두르 + 어요 → 서둘러요, and the past is 서둘렀어요 — anchor everything on 서둘러요. The classic English-speaker mistake is regularizing it to 서두러요 (no doubled ㄹ). Collocations: 서둘러 나가다 (hurry out), 서두르다가 넘어지다 (trip from rushing), 서두를 거 없어요 (no need to rush).

usage: to wander lost looking for the way
to wander for a good while
한참 'quite a while' is the habitual time word here
골목 'back alley' — the maze you get lost in
to flounder, unable to find the answer
Figurative: to be at a loss / struggle
examples: 길을 헤맸어요.
I wandered around lost.
Simplest: 길 + 을, with the contracted past 헤맸어요
주소를 몰라서 골목을 한참 헤맸어요.
I didn't know the address so I wandered the alleys for ages.
Everyday: cause 몰라서 + 한참 + 을 marking the wandered space
출구를 못 찾아서 큰 역에서 30분이나 헤맸어요.
I couldn't find the exit so I wandered a huge station for a whole 30 minutes.
Real situation: 못 찾다 cause + emphatic 30분이나 'as much as 30 min'
nuance: 헤매다 means to wander about lost, roaming without finding your way — and by extension to flounder or struggle when you can't find a solution. The contrast to nail is against 산책하다 ('to take a stroll'), which is pleasant and purposeful: a 산책 is relaxing, but 헤매다 carries frustration and being lost. Don't confuse it with the similar-sounding 헤어지다 ('to break up / part ways') — totally different meaning. Register is plain and everyday. The place or route you wander through takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 헤매다), which surprises English speakers who expect a location particle like 에서 — but here the path is treated as the thing you traverse. As a verb stem ending in ㅐ, the vowel contractions are clean: 헤매 + 어요 → 헤매요, and the past 헤매 + 었어요 → 헤맸어요 (double ㅆ). Collocations: 길을 헤매다, 정신없이 헤매다 (wander in a daze), 헤매고 다니다 (roam around lost). Pitfall: learners say 길에서 헤매다, but the idiomatic frame is 길을 헤매다.

usage: The place you drop into takes 에 (destination of the brief visit)
to stop by on the way
가는 길에 'on the way there' is the signature collocation
to drop by for a moment
잠깐 'briefly' underscores the short, in-passing nature
to swing by home and then go
-았다 가다 = stop somewhere en route to elsewhere
examples: 마트에 들러요.
I stop by the mart.
Simplest: place 마트 + 에 with the ㅡ-irregular form 들러요
집에 가기 전에 약국에 잠깐 들렀어요.
I stopped by the pharmacy briefly before going home.
Everyday: -기 전에 'before' + 잠깐, past 들렀어요
근처 오면 우리 집에 꼭 들러요.
If you're nearby, definitely swing by our place.
Real situation: friendly invitation, 꼭 'for sure' + the casual command 들러요
nuance: 들르다 means to stop by / drop in somewhere briefly while on your way to another destination — the visit is short and incidental, not the main purpose of the trip. Contrast it with 방문하다 ('to visit', Sino-Korean 訪問), which is a planned, often formal visit you make for its own sake: you 방문하다 a client's office on purpose, but you 들르다 a convenience store because it's on the route. Register is casual and warm; 가는 길에 들러요 is exactly how a friend invites you over. The brief-visit destination takes 에 (집에 들르다). The whole difficulty is the conjugation: 들르다 is a ㅡ (eu) irregular — before a vowel ending the final ㅡ simply drops with NO doubled ㄹ (unlike 르-irregular verbs), so 들르 + 어요 → 들러요 and the past is 들렀어요. Collocations: 잠깐 들르다, 들렀다 가다, 가는 길에 들르다.

usage: The institution you're late TO takes 에
지각 can split from 하다 and take 을 as a noun
지각 한 번 counts tardies, as at school/work
examples: 학교에 지각했어요.
I was late to school.
Simplest: institution 학교 + 에, past 지각했어요
늦잠을 자서 회사에 지각했어요.
I overslept so I was late to work.
Everyday: cause 늦잠을 자다 'oversleep' + the 하다 verb past
한 번만 더 지각하면 결석으로 처리돼요.
If you're late just one more time it'll be counted as an absence.
Real situation: institutional consequence, 결석 'absence' contrast
nuance: 지각하다 is Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'late-moment') + 하다, meaning specifically to arrive late to an appointed place like school, work, or a meeting — it is the institutional 'tardy', the kind a teacher or boss notes. The vital contrast is with the adjective 늦다 ('to be late' in general): 늦다 covers ANY lateness ('the bus is late', 'I'm running late', 늦어서 미안해요), whereas 지각하다 is narrowly being tardy to a fixed obligation. So 'sorry I'm late' to a friend is 늦어서 미안해요, never 지각해서; save 지각하다 for school/office tardiness. Register is neutral-formal, with a school/workplace flavor. The place you're late to takes 에 (회사에 지각하다). As a 하다 verb, the negative and potential split the noun off: 지각 안 해요, 지각 못 해요 — not 안 지각해요. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly using 지각하다 for every 'I'm late', when most casual lateness should be plain 늦다.

usage: to go meet someone at the airport
The pickup spot takes 에; classic airport-greeting frame
to go out to meet/pick up
마중 + 나가다 is the most idiomatic everyday form
마중 + 을 가다 = head out for the pickup
The arriving person you greet takes 을/를
examples: 친구를 마중해요.
I go to meet my friend.
Simplest: person 친구 + 를, the 하다 verb 마중해요
어머니가 역까지 저를 마중 나오셨어요.
My mother came out all the way to the station to meet me.
Everyday: 마중 나오다 form + honorific -시- for an elder
손님이 도착하면 제가 공항으로 마중 갈게요.
When the guest arrives I'll go to the airport to pick them up.
Real situation: 도착하다 'arrive' + the offer 마중 갈게요
nuance: 마중하다 is native Korean 마중 ('a going-out to receive an arriver') + 하다, meaning to go out and greet/pick up someone who is arriving — at a station, airport, or your door. Its exact antonym is 배웅하다 ('to see someone off' as they LEAVE): you 마중하다 an arrival and 배웅하다 a departure, and confusing the two reverses the whole scene. It carries a warm, caring connotation — going out of your way to welcome someone — and is neutral-to-warm in register. The person you greet takes 을/를 (친구를 마중하다), and the spot takes 에 or directional 으로 (공항으로 마중 가다). In real speech the standalone verb 마중하다 is actually less common than the collocations 마중 나가다 / 마중 나오다 / 마중 가다 ('go/come out to meet'), so learn those phrasal forms. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 마중 안 해요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 만나다 ('to meet'): 만나다 is meeting on equal footing anywhere, but 마중하다 specifically means going TO the arrival point to receive someone — and don't mix it up with 마치다 ('to finish'), which only sounds similar.
